Pfund.et: From Middle High German pfunt, phunt, from Old High German pfunt, phunt, from Proto-West Germanic *pund, from Proto-Germanic *pundą, a borrowing from Latin pondō (“by weight”, adverb) or Latin pondus (“weight”, noun).

s: an exclamation of disgust, aversion, dislike, contempt, or annoyance
pfui.et: From Middle High German pfui, phiu, probably imitative of spitting out.

Pfütze.et: From Middle High German pfütze, from Old High German pfuzzi, from Proto-West Germanic *puti (“a well”). Doublet of Pütz (“well; bucket”) and Pütt (“mine shaft”).

Pfurz.et: From Middle High German vurz, from Old High German furz, from Proto-West Germanic *furtu. Upper German variant of Furz. Compare Bavarian Pfurz.

s: Nach der zweiten Maß war das Volksfest aber eigentlich doch ganz pfundig.
great-great-grandfather (an ancestor of five generations ago or beyond)
Pfuchahn.et: pfuch + Ahn, in use in the 17th and 18th centuries, by the 20th century dialectal or obsolete. Pfuch is probably an interjection of disgust like pfui! (“fie”). It is unclear whether this is the actual etymology or just a folk etymological reinterpretation.

Pfuhl.et: From Middle High German pfuol, from Old High German pfuol, from Proto-West Germanic *pōl, from Proto-Germanic *pōlaz. Akin to English pool and Dutch poel.

s: Die Handwerker haben beim Bau gepfuscht.
The workers botched their job during the construction.
to cheat; to avoid or break the rules (e.g. in school)
